metadata.title: Digit Counts, Logarithmic Sums, and Integrated Patterns
metadata.description: Use logarithms to count digits and simplify multi-step products, telescoping expressions, and integrated logarithm patterns.
metadata.teachingApproach: Develop definitions and laws step by step, explain why each transformation is valid, show intermediate calculations and checks, and use targeted practice with changed-value remedial retries.
metadata.sourceScope: R.S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude for Competitive Examinations, Chapter 10 “Logarithms,” printed pages 297–307. Approved scope: Teach the digit-count rule for a positive integer N: digits=floor(log_10 N)+1, with an explicit boundary check when N is an exact power of 10. Estimate logs of large powers from supplied common logs; include products such as 4^m·5^n by combining logs and confirming the integer boundary. Also teach source-supported telescoping products of chained logarithms, sums of common logs over consecutive factors, and integrated expressions that require at least two earlier skills. Distinguish a logarithm's characteristic from the digit count and preserve exactness or show rounding safeguards.

content.text: Welcome to Digit Counts, Logarithmic Sums, and Integrated Patterns. Use logarithms to count digits and simplify multi-step products, telescoping expressions, and integrated logarithm patterns.

Integrated problems usually become manageable when classified before calculation. Ask: is this an evaluation, an equation, a change-of-base chain, or a common-log computation? Then choose the inverse definition or law that exposes the structure.
A useful first move is domain. If variables occur inside logs, record every positivity condition and intersect them. For log_2(x−1)+log_2(5−x), both arguments must be positive, so 1<x<5.

After domain, look for inverse cancellation. log_3(3^x)=x is immediate for real x because 3^x is positive and base 3 is valid. In a more complicated equation, do not cancel across addition or across a mismatched base.
A chain product can connect a distant base to a final argument: log_2(3)·log_3(5)·log_5(16)=log_2(16)=4. The intermediate bases telescope; they do not disappear from unrelated sums.
When different logarithms are added, first see whether exact values are available. log_2(8)+log_4(16)=3+2=5. Combining them as a single log would be invalid because the bases differ.

If the bases differ but the equation is simple, convert to a common base. For log_4(x)=3, use x=4³. If a numeric log is needed, use supplied values or a calculator only when the task allows approximation.
Example: solve log_2(x−1)+log_2(x+1)=3. Domain x>1. Combine to log_2(x²−1)=3, giving x²−1=8. Candidate roots ±3; retain x=3 and verify log_2 2 + log_2 4 =1+2=3.

The check in that example catches a common error: using only the product equation can preserve a root outside the original domain. Every original log argument must be checked independently, not just their product.
For a positive integer N, digits=floor(log_10(N))+1. A d-digit integer satisfies 10^(d−1)≤N<10^d, which proves the rule. At an exact power of ten, the same formula still gives k+1 digits for N=10^k.

Check exact boundaries explicitly. 1000=10^3 has log 3 and 4 digits; a number just below 1000 has logarithm below 3 and 3 digits. Never round a logarithm before taking its floor when it may be close to an integer.
Example: with log(2)=0.3010, log(2^20)=20(0.3010)=6.0200. Thus 2^20 has floor(6.0200)+1=7 digits. The size check 10^6<2^20<10^7 confirms the count.

For a product such as 4^m·5^n, add logs: m log(4)+n log(5). Use log(4)=2log(2) and log(5)=1−log(2) when log(2) is supplied. Preserve enough digits before taking the floor; small rounding errors matter near a power of 10.

A consecutive product can be converted to a sum of logs: log(2)+log(3)+…+log(9)=log(2·3·…·9). This is the logarithm of a product, not a sum of the original factors. Factor or estimate the product only as the task requires.
Change of base is a bridge, not a new rule for arbitrary manipulation. log_a(x)=log_b(x)/log_b(a); verify numerator/denominator by setting x=a, which must yield 1.
An exact expression can be more informative than a decimal. log_3(6) is a valid exact value even when it is not an integer. Do not force it into a guessed integer, and do not round unless asked.

Three-term expressions can test whether a learner distinguishes laws. Expand log_a(x²y/z) as 2log_a(x)+log_a(y)−log_a(z), with x,y,z positive. Reverse the process by checking each coefficient and sign.

When a problem mixes laws and equations, preserve the original form for the final substitution. A transformed equation may be algebraically equivalent only under the recorded domain and any nonzero conditions used in manipulation.

Finish with four checks: base validity, argument positivity, exact algebra, and magnitude/sign. For approximate common-log work, include the supplied precision and verify the answer lies in the correct power-of-ten interval.

For an integer N, d digits means 10^(d−1)≤N<10^d. Taking common logarithms gives d−1≤log(N)<d, so d=floor(log(N))+1. The strict upper bound explains why an exact power of 10 has one more digit than its exponent.

A rounded logarithm near an integer deserves extra care. If log(N) is estimated as 5.000 from rounded data, that alone may not show whether N is just below or exactly at 10^5. Use exact factorization or a sufficiently precise bound before deciding the floor.

For 4^m·5^n, the product has a useful structure because 4 and 5 complement to 20, not 10. Combine logarithms exactly: m·2log(2)+n·(1−log(2)); then evaluate with supplied precision and check the resulting power-of-ten interval.

Telescoping products and sums obey different rules. A product log_a(b)·log_b(c) collapses to log_a(c). A sum log(x)+log(y) becomes log(xy). Never cancel adjacent bases in a sum; identify the outer operation first.

To estimate a consecutive-factor sum, combine it before calculating: log(2)+log(3)+log(4)+log(5)=log(120). With supplied values, this is log(2)+log(3)+2log(2)+log(5), which can be checked against 100<120<1000.
